what_it_does: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is a computing style inspired loosely by how brains work: instead of precise numbers, data is represented as extremely long bit strings (tens of thousands of bits — called 'hypervectors') and operations like addition and comparison on these strings are highly parallel and error-tolerant. HDC is appealing for hardware because it is cheap and robust, but running graph neural networks — AI models that reason over structured data like social networks or molecules — on HDC is hard because standard HDC hypervectors distort node features, are biased by graph structure, and miss information about individual nodes. CiliaGraph fixes all three problems: it redesigns the HDC encoding and aggregation steps so graph structure is correctly captured without feature distortion, and it adds a supervision signal for individual nodes. Crucially, it achieves this with much shorter hypervectors (hundreds of bits instead of tens of thousands), which dramatically reduces the memory needed. Exact accuracy and efficiency numbers are not confirmed from the abstract.
